title: We interviewed Devil Wears Prada in real life
guest: Leah Wyar, President of Beauty, Style and Entertainment brands at Dotdash Meredith (People, Entertainment Weekly, InStyle, Byrdie, Brides, People en Espanol)
summary: Media executive Leah Wyar explains how a beauty editor role is really a business and marketing role, why work wives and long-term female friendships are a survival mechanism and a leadership style, and how she navigates workplace politics as an emotional, energy-sensitive leader. She shares her 'just say yes' philosophy that led her to run the entertainment group, her 21-year partnership with a supportive younger husband, and her painful multi-year IVF journey before conceiving naturally.

ideas.idea: A beauty editor is a revenue-driving business role, not just creative play: you must know your advertisers and craft ideas live in the room that serve both the brand's customer and your reader.
ideas.detail: At Cosmo, beauty drove so much revenue that Leah reported almost equally to the editor in chief and the publisher, sitting in live brainstorms with CMOs from P&G, Unilever and L'Oreal who wanted a first-to-market idea, not a recycled one. She realized that if she got really good at this she could have a very long-lasting career.

ideas.idea: You have to be as much of an expert about your reader as about the partner across the table; the magic moment is when one idea serves both.
ideas.detail: Leah says there were 3 or 4 moments in her career where she 'nailed it' this way and she got addicted to that feeling, which is what she wanted to keep doing as long as possible.

ideas.idea: Work wives are a survival mechanism: you spend most of your life with your work family, and you need people to vent, cry and be real with to get through hard stretches without resentment.
ideas.detail: Jumping ship rarely resolves frustration because you find the same frustrations elsewhere; a trusted colleague helps you flow into the next stage. Cherie recalls rage-quit moments at Zynga with her work wife Maya solved by a venting walk and a 3-minute hug.

ideas.idea: Decades-long work friendships become therapists and shorthand partners; even a supportive husband 'gets it but doesn't get it' like your girls at work do.
ideas.detail: Leah's friends Holly, Meredith, Melissa and Jo have moved companies together since Cosmo. Her therapist prescribes a walk with a friend or a 3-minute hug in eject-button weeks.

ideas.idea: Being openly grateful and affectionate with female colleagues is a distinct leadership style: disagreement framed as 'I love you, but let's sit on this one thing' gets people to a middle ground and trickles down into a more collaborative team.
ideas.detail: Leah contrasts this with the era 10 years ago when women felt they had to be tough like men with an 'alpha' undertone; you can be direct with feedback without that energy, and teams now expect and respect it.

ideas.idea: Life motto 'just say yes': saying yes to things you don't feel like doing is what creates the serendipitous moments that change your life.
ideas.detail: The advice came from a boss after a breakup at 30. Leah met her husband at a Halloween party she almost skipped, and got her first job by tossing a resume she had 'no business' submitting into a folder. Saying no too much means you're not going anywhere or meeting anyone.

ideas.idea: When someone sees a capability in you that you don't see in yourself, trust it and try; you would not have raised your hand for it on your own.
ideas.detail: After 20+ years in beauty, Leah initially said no when her boss asked her to run the entertainment group (People, EW, People en Espanol) after the Meredith acquisition; she slept on it, said yes, and calls it the best decision she ever made even though it was really hard.

ideas.idea: Reframe risk as 'what's the best that can happen': if the new role fails you can go back to what you did before, but if it succeeds you learn an entire new business.
ideas.detail: Leah told herself that if she didn't succeed in entertainment she could return to beauty; the hosts relate this to their own leap from tech into podcasting and a physical product (Sisters Matcha).

ideas.idea: Your best ideas come in the shower or in the 10 minutes before sleep and after waking, when there are no incoming inputs; the difference is actually acting on them.
ideas.detail: Once you've taken an idea from brain to finished thing once, you have a playbook and the confidence you can do it again; 'that's the secret to it all.'

ideas.idea: There is beauty in being naive: switching from print to digital was like on-the-job postgraduate work, emailing herself 'Google this later' and relying on smart people around her.
ideas.detail: She is now launching an app knowing nothing about apps; you can figure it out if you give up control and spread empowerment so everyone does what they're best at. She credits the familial leadership at her company for letting her succeed this way.

ideas.idea: Workplace politics starts in middle management, where you are the jelly in the sandwich policing what comes down from your boss and up from your team, and must learn to lead with influence rather than force.
ideas.detail: Early years are about developing thick skin in a cutthroat publishing industry; later the hard question becomes when to side with your team versus your boss.

ideas.idea: Do not assume the boss you do dirty work for will protect you forever; one day they are gone and you lose your direct line overnight.
ideas.detail: At Cosmo, Leah had a direct line to the chief content officer and 24 hours later was under new leadership she had no relationship with; she concluded the company's direction was no longer for her and left.

ideas.idea: Once you have kids, a paycheck is not enough: you must feel respected, keep learning and see a future path, and when that stops you have to go.
ideas.detail: If she's leaving her kids for 9 hours a day she has to feel fulfilled; she could have toughed out Cosmo another year or two with her thick skin but would not have been happy.

ideas.idea: Don't let anyone weaponize you and take the emotion out: when your CEO dislikes something, he dislikes what's on paper, not you; feedback is meant to make you better even when delivered badly.
ideas.detail: After 25 years working she still practices this daily. Compartmentalize the energy, box it up on a shelf, find the fixable core of the feedback, and don't treat it as a crystal ball saying you don't belong.

ideas.idea: Being highly sensitive to a room's energy is a blessing and a curse: it lets you read and respond in real time without a script, but makes it hard not to take things personally.
ideas.detail: Leah says she is not a stoic leader; she goes in with a loose outline and reads what's going on. Sporadic difficult people can be steeled against, but being in that energy constantly is not OK.

ideas.idea: Therapy gives you a toolkit: workplace reactions to tone and energy trace back to childhood experiences, and naming their source lets you control the cortisol rush instead of panicking.
ideas.detail: Leah didn't think she needed a therapist before 2001 and now says it changed her life; she traced a reaction back to 8th-grade friends dropping her. The first 18 years are so impressionable that these moments erupt in the workplace in weird ways.

ideas.idea: Men with finance backgrounds give direct rather than flowery feedback, and learning not to take that personally has helped her thrive under male bosses for the first time.
ideas.detail: The last 5 years are the first time she has had male bosses (three of them); some past female bosses had even harder delivery, but the style difference forced her to separate feedback from self-worth.

ideas.idea: Show up unemotional in the room and get it done, because you have an 'underbelly' of work wives, husband and therapist where you can rage and be raw afterward.
ideas.detail: During a crunch app launch (T-minus 2 weeks) she absorbs hard feedback stone-faced, locks in, walks out, takes a rage walk, and relies on muscle memory that she has seen this pattern through a million times.

ideas.idea: Choose a partner who wants you to be as or more successful than they are; the crux of a partnership is allowing each person to thrive, leapfrogging each other without competition.
ideas.detail: Leah dated people who didn't want an equal or more successful partner, and those relationships ended. Her husband Nick, 5 years younger and raised by a single mom to respect women, loved that she was many levels ahead in her career; together 21 years since 2004, now both running businesses and trading childcare when the other travels.

ideas.idea: She knew her husband was 'the one' the day she met him and called her aunt the next day to say so, despite him being 22 and her 27.
ideas.detail: Over time you come to understand the depths of why that cosmic first impression was right, in her case his deep support for her ambitions.

ideas.idea: Advice to her younger self: don't assume that because something came easily once it will always be easy; life includes mountains you can't will your way over.
ideas.detail: She got pregnant the first time she tried in her mid-30s, then went through rounds and rounds of failed IVF for her second child and was depressed for a couple of years before giving up, then conceived her daughter naturally. Her gynecologist joked it was an 'egg exfoliation.'

ideas.idea: As women, we deal with biology that competes with career growth, and there is no universal formula; it's a bespoke problem each woman solves with her friends, work wives, therapy and resilience toolkit.
ideas.detail: Even with a partner who cries every ounce of it with you, women take fertility struggles as their own fault; Leah calls it 'our blessing and our burden at the same time.'
